newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania pins NATO entry hopes on French support.
newsitem.headline: Romania pins NATO entry hopes on French support.

text.p: Romania's new centrist leadership hopes that a visit by French President Jacques Chirac starting on Friday will help to catapult the ex-communist country into the fast lane towards an expanded NATO.
President Emil Constantinescu, in an interview published on Thursday, said there was no strategic sense in leaving Romania out of a first wave of NATO expansion to be announced in July.
"From a military and strategic point of view, the expansion of NATO without Bucharest would have no meaning," he told the Paris daily Le Figaro.
Constantinescu will extend a red-carpet welcome to Chirac, the most senior Western leader to visit the Balkan state since his late Socialist predecessor Francois Mitterrand in 1991.
Chirac has openly backed Romania's outsider bid to be considered for early membership along with favourites Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.

But U.S. officials accompanying Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on a European tour said Romania was still a "long shot" behind the three favourites even if its prospects, and those of Slovenia, appeared to have improved.
Chirac said Russia was linking the admission of up to five new members to a separate accord with NATO taking account of its security interests.

"Either there is this accord and they (Russia) are ready to accept the admission to NATO of three, four or five countries, or there is no accord and then they will oppose the expansion of the alliance," he told the Bucharest daily Adevarul.

Moscow had no objections to Romanian membership, Chirac said, adding: "The Russians will not pose difficulties for Romania...For NATO, it (Romania) is very important, especially for the southern flank of the alliance."

Russia has repeatedly opposed NATO's eastward expansion. But Foreign Ministry spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said before Albright arrived in Moscow that a separate accord would "reduce to a minimum the unavoidable negative consequences of the bloc's expansion."
Romanian leaders hope France will help to exploit their country's strategic position on the Black Sea to create a land corridor towards Poland, along with ex-Soviet Ukraine.

"Romania has a privileged position and can enhance European stability, considering the recent turmoil around us, in Serbia, Albania, Bulgaria and even tension between Greece and Turkey," said Senate chairman Petre Roman, a former prime minister
"Romania could form a triangle with Poland and Ukraine and work like a shield of stability in the region."
Romania hopes France can sway a sceptical Washington into agreeing to include Romania among the first new NATO entrants.
"If France and the United States discuss this it can only lead to the result we expected," said Roman, number two in the state hierarchy. "Both the French and Americans would win."
Chirac's two-day visit includes an address to parliament's two chambers on Saturday and a question-and-answer meeting with Bucharest University students.

France helped to create modern Romania by supporting the union of the principalities of Wallachia and Moldavia and then helping the emergence of Greater Romania in 1918 when Transylvania joined the kingdom.
Bucharest pledged tough reforms this week to bridge an economic gap with Hungary, its more advanced neighbour.
Chirac praised Romania's conclusion of a treaty last year settling border and ethnic minority disputes with Hungary and he called for efforts to reach a similar accord with Ukraine.
